# Large Sample Inference {#sec-lsinf}

The asymptotic results for the OLS estimator in this chapter follow Chapter 2 of @Hayashi2000.

@sec-ssinf gave us *exact* finite-sample inference ($t$-tests, $F$-tests, confidence intervals) for $\hat\beta,$ but only under Assumption 4$^\ast$ of @sec-ssinf:

* errors $\varepsilon_i$ are **normally distributed**, and
* errors are **spherical** (homoskedastic and uncorrelated).

Real data rarely satisfies either requirement exactly.

For a sufficiently **large** sample size $n$, we can drop *both* requirements and still do (approximately) valid inference about $\beta$. This chapter shows why, and how.

## Why Large Samples Help

Two classical results from probability theory do essentially all of the work:

* The **Law of Large Numbers (LLN)**: sample means stabilize around their population mean as $n$ grows.
* The **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**: suitably scaled sample means become approximately normally distributed as $n$ grows -- regardless of how the underlying data are distributed.

::: {.callout icon=false}
#
::: {#thm-SLLN1}
## Law of Large Numbers (by Kolmogorov)



If $Z_1,\dots,Z_n$ is an i.i.d. sequence with $E(Z_i)=\mu$, then the sample mean
$$
\bar{Z}_n:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i
$$
gets arbitrarily close to $\mu$ as $n\to\infty$. We write
$$
\bar{Z}_n\to_{p}\mu,\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty,
$$
read "$\bar{Z}_n$ converges in probability to $\mu$."
:::
:::

@fig-LLN illustrates what "converges in probability" means: pick any corridor $\mu\pm\epsilon$ around the limit using some (small) $\epsilon>0.$ For small $n$, many paths of $\bar{Z}_n$ lie outside it. As $n$ grows, the probability that $\bar{Z}_n$ lies outside the corridor shrinks to zero, i.e. $P\left(|\bar{Z}_n-\mu|>\epsilon\right)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, and this holds for every $\epsilon>0,$ no matter how small.

```{r}
#| label: fig-LLN
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-retina: 1
#| fig-keep: all
#| animation-hook: gifski
#| interval: 0.15
#| fig-cap: "Law of Large Numbers: running sample means $\\bar{Z}_n$ of 30 independent sequences of fair-die rolls, $E(Z_i)=\\mu=3.5$. As $n$ grows, the paths settle into the corridor $\\mu\\pm\\varepsilon$ (green lines) and stay there; the dots mark each path's current value (green: inside, red: outside the corridor)."
set.seed(321)

## Z_i: rolls of a fair die, i.e. mu = E(Z_i) = 3.5
mu    <- 3.5
eps   <- 0.25
M     <- 30                                   # number of sample-mean paths
n_max <- 1000
Z     <- matrix(sample(1:6, n_max * M, replace = TRUE), nrow = n_max)
Zbar  <- apply(Z, 2, cumsum) / (1:n_max)      # running sample means

## animation frames: sample sizes on a log grid, then pause on n = n_max
n_grid <- unique(round(10^seq(0, log10(n_max), length.out = 40)))
n_hold <- 12

## solid colours only: GIFs have no partial transparency
col_path <- "steelblue"
col_in   <- "forestgreen"
col_out  <- "red"

for(f in seq_len(length(n_grid) + n_hold)){
  n      <- n_grid[min(f, length(n_grid))]
  hold   <- f > length(n_grid)
  inside <- abs(Zbar[n, ] - mu) <= eps
  plot(NA, xlim = c(1, n_max), ylim = c(1, 6), log = "x", las = 1,
       xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "",
       main = bquote("Sample means" ~ bar(Z)[n] ~ "of" ~ .(M) ~
                     "independent samples (here: die rolls)"))
  matlines(1:n, Zbar[1:n, , drop = FALSE], lty = 1, lwd = 1.2, col = col_path)
  abline(h = mu, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5, col = par("fg"))
  abline(h = mu + c(-eps, eps), lwd = 2.5, col = col_in)
  points(rep(n, M), Zbar[n, ], pch = 19, cex = 1.2,
         col = ifelse(inside, col_in, col_out))
  legend("topright", bty = "n", text.col = par("fg"),
         legend = c(bquote(mu == .(mu)),
                    bquote("Corridor" ~ mu %+-% epsilon ~ "with" ~ epsilon == .(eps)),
                    bquote("n =" ~ .(n) * ":" ~ .(sum(inside)) ~ "of" ~ .(M) ~
                           "paths inside the corridor")),
         lty = c(2, 1, NA), lwd = c(1.5, 2.5, NA),
         col = c(par("fg"), col_in, NA))
  if(hold){
    text(n_max, 1.4, adj = 1, cex = 1.2, col = par("fg"),
         labels = bquote(P(abs(bar(Z)[n] - mu) > epsilon) %->% 0 ~ "as" ~ n %->% infinity))
    ## invisible, frame-specific point: knitr would otherwise merge the
    ## identical pause frames into one
    points(1, 1, col = NA, cex = f)
  }
}
```

::: {.callout icon=false}
#
::: {#thm-CLT1}
## Central Limit Theorem (Lindeberg-Lévy)


If $Z_1,\dots,Z_n$ is an i.i.d. sequence with $E(Z_i)=\mu$ and $Var(Z_i)=\sigma^2$, then the **distribution** of the appropriately centered and scaled sample mean
$$
\sqrt{n}\big(\bar{Z}_n-\mu\big)
$$
gets arbitrarily close to a normal distribution; i.e.
$$
\sqrt{n}(\bar{Z}_n-\mu)\to_{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$
That is, for large $n$, the (appropriately scaled) sample mean is **approximately normally distributed** -- no matter what distribution the $Z_i$ themselves have.
:::
:::

<!-- 
::: {.callout-tip}
A full treatment of stochastic convergence -- the different modes of convergence (in probability, almost surely, in mean square, in distribution), the Continuous Mapping Theorem, Slutsky's theorem, the Cramér-Wold device, and more general LLN/CLT variants (e.g., for heterogeneously distributed or weakly dependent data) -- is kept in the archived, theory-heavy version of this chapter, `07-Asymptotics_OLD.qmd`, in the repository.
::: 
-->

Together, the LLN and CLT give us everything we need to show that $\hat\beta_n$ is:

1. **consistent**: $\hat\beta_n$ gets arbitrarily close to $\beta$ as $n\to\infty$, and
2. **asymptotically normal**: $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_n-\beta)$ is approximately normal for large $n$,

*without* requiring that the error terms $\varepsilon_i$ themselves are normally distributed.

## Asymptotics under the Classic Regression Model

Two OLS estimators:
$$
\hat\beta_n=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}Y
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
s^2_{ub,n}=\frac{1}{n-K}\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\epsilon_i^2.
$$

* Both are **consistent**.
* $\hat\beta_n$ is **asymptotically normal**.

$\Rightarrow$ We can drop the normality and spherical-errors assumption (Assumption 4$^\ast$ of @sec-ssinf) -- and still use our inference tools ($t$-tests, $F$-tests) from @sec-ssinf, as long as $n$ is "large."

**Notation:** split $\hat\beta_n$ into its building blocks.
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta_n
&=\left(X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}X^{\top}Y\\[2ex]
&\text{expanding by $\frac{1}{n}\colon$}\\[2ex]
&=\left(\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}Y\\[2ex]
&\text{using $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon\colon$}\\[2ex]
&=\left(\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}(X\beta + \varepsilon)\\[2ex]
&\text{multiplying out:}\\[2ex]
&=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}X}_{=I_K}\;\;\beta + \left(\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon\\[2ex]
&=\beta + \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X\right)^{-1}}_{=S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}}\;\;\;\;\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon\\[2ex]
&=\beta + \;\;\;\;\;\;S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$
with
\begin{align*}
\underset{(K\times K)}{S_{X^{\top}X}} &:= \frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_iX_i^{\top}\\[2ex]
\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\varepsilon.
\end{align*}


The mean of the $(K\times 1)$ vector $X_{i} \varepsilon_i$ is given by
\begin{align*}
E\left(X_{i} \varepsilon_i\right)
&=E\left(E\left(X_{i} \varepsilon_i\mid X\right)\right)\\[2ex]
&=E\left(X_i \;E\left(\varepsilon_i\mid X\right)\right)\\[2ex]
&=E\left(X_i\;\underbrace{E\left(\varepsilon_i\mid X\right)}_{=0}\right)\\[2ex]
&=E\left(X_i\;0\;\right) = E(0) = \underset{(K\times 1)}{0}.
\end{align*}

Thus, by the LLN, $\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i} \varepsilon_i$ converges (in probability) to a $(K\times 1)$ zero vector $0,$
$$
\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i} \varepsilon_i \to_p 0 \quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$


Let denote the mean of the $(K\times K)$ matrix $X_iX_i^\top$ by
$$
E\left(X_iX_i^\top\right) =: \Sigma_{X^{\top}X}. 
$$

Thus, by the LLN, $S_{X^{\top}X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_iX_i^{\top}$ converges (in probability) to its population limit $E\left(X_iX_i^{\top}\right)=\Sigma_{X^{\top}X},$
$$
S_{X^{\top}X}= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_iX_i^{\top} \to_p E\left(X_iX_i^{\top}\right)=\Sigma_{X^{\top}X} \quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$

Eventually, we need to invert the population limit quantity $\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}.$ Therefore, we have to restate the full-rank assumption (Assumption 3 of @sec-MLR) for $\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}\colon$



**Assumption 3$^\ast$: (Population) Rank Condition**

The $(K\times K)$ matrix
$$
\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}=E(S_{X^{\top}X})
$$
has full rank $K$. I.e., $\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}$ is nonsingular and invertible.


#### **Showing Consistency of $\widehat{\beta}_n$** {-}

Now, we have everything to argue that $\widehat{\beta}_n$ is consistent for $\beta;$ i.e. that 
$$
\widehat{\beta}_n\to_{p}\beta\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty
$$
as stated below in @thm-bconsistent1. 

By the LLN, $\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i} \varepsilon_i$ is consistent for the $(K\times 1)$ zero vector $0\colon$
$$
\frac{1}{n} X^{\top}\varepsilon = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i} \varepsilon_i\to_{p} \underset{(K\times 1)}{0} \quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$

By the LLN, $S_{X^{\top}X}$ is consistent for $(K\times K)$ matrix $\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}$:
$$
S_{X^{\top}X}\to_{p}\underset{(K\times K)}{\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}}\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$
By another result, the **Continuous Mapping Theorem**, we may take the inverse and the product of these limits, so that, as $n\to\infty,$
$$
\widehat{\beta}_n=\beta + S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\;\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\varepsilon_i \to_p \beta + \Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}0=\beta.
$$


::: {.callout icon=false}
#
::: {#thm-bconsistent1}
## Consistency of $\hat\beta$

Under Assumptions 1, 2, 3$^\ast$, and 4, and under the assumption that $X_i$ has finite second moments, and $\varepsilon_i$ has finite first moments, we have that
$$
\hat\beta_n\to_{p}\beta\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$
:::
:::

The appropriately scaled OLS estimator is also **asymptotically normal**. We state this first for the homoskedastic case; the heteroskedastic case follows in @sec-CaseHetero.

::: {.callout icon=false}
#
::: {#thm-OLSnormality1}
## Asymptotic Normality of $\hat{\beta}$ (Homoskedastic Case)
Under Assumption 1, 2, 3$^\ast$, and 4, and under the assumption that $X_i$ and $\varepsilon_i$ have finite second moments, and under the simplifying assumption of spherical errors
$$
Var(\varepsilon|X)=\sigma^2I_n,
$$
we have that
$$
\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_n-\beta)\to_{d} \mathcal{N}_K\left(0,\sigma^2 \Sigma^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right),\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty,
$$
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 \Sigma^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}
& = \lim_{n\to\infty} Var\left(\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_n-\beta)\right)\\[2ex]
& = \lim_{n\to\infty} n Var\left(\hat\beta_n\right)\\[2ex]
& = \operatorname{AVar}(\hat\beta_n)
\end{aligned}
$$
is the asymptotic variance of $\hat\beta_n.$
:::
:::

By @thm-OLSnormality1, for spherical errors and largish $n$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_n-\beta)&\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}_K\left(0,\sigma^2 \Sigma^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right)\\[2ex]
\Rightarrow\qquad\hat\beta_n &\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}_K\left(\beta, n^{-1}\sigma^2 \Sigma^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
The approximation error vanishes as $n\to\infty.$

We don't know $\operatorname{AVar}(\hat\beta_n) = \sigma^2\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}$ -- plug in the consistent estimator
$$
\widehat{\operatorname{AVar}}(\hat\beta_n) = s_{ub}^2 S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}.
$$
(Both $S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}$ and $s_{ub}^2$ are consistent, by the LLN.)

### The Case of Heteroskedasticity {#sec-CaseHetero}

An asymptotic (large $n$) normality result as in @thm-OLSnormality1 can also be derived for conditionally **heteroskedastic** error terms. For largish $n\colon$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_n-\beta)\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}_K\left(0,\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\right)\\[2ex]
\Rightarrow\qquad\hat\beta_n\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}_K\left(\beta,n^{-1}\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-OLSnormality1Rob}
The approximation error vanishes as $n\to\infty.$

**Key takeaway:**

* Valid inference **without** assuming homoskedasticity.
* We only need a good estimator of the "sandwiched" middle term $E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})$ in
$$
\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}.
$$
* That estimator is the subject of the rest of this chapter.

## Robust Standard Errors

We need a consistent estimator of
$$
E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top}).
$$
The following **Heteroskedasticity Consistent (HC)** estimators are commonly used:

HC-Type  | Formula
------|------------
HC0   |$\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\varepsilon_i^2X_iX_i^{\top}$
HC1   | $\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{n}{n-K}\hat\varepsilon_i^2X_iX_i^{\top}$
HC2   | $\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}}{1-h_{i}}X_iX_i^{\top}$
HC3   | $\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}}{\left(1-h_{i}\right)^{2}}X_iX_i^{\top}$
HC4    | $\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}}{\left(1-h_{i}\right)^{\delta_{i}}}X_iX_i^{\top}$ with $\delta_i=\min\{4,,h_i/\bar h\}$

**HC3** is the most commonly used HC-estimator.

::: {.callout-tip}
The **leverage statistic** of $X_i$: $h_i:=[P_X]_{ii}$.

* $1/n\leq h_i\leq 1$
* average leverage: $\bar{h}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nh_i=K/n$

* **High leverage**: $h_i\gg K/n$ -- $X_i$ sits far from the other $X_j$'s.
* **Influential outlier**: high leverage *and* large $|\hat\varepsilon_i|$ -- distorts $\hat\beta_n$.
* HC2--HC4 upweight residuals at high-leverage points to compensate.
:::

* **HC0:** @White1980; justified asymptotically.
* **HC1--HC3:** @MacKinnon_White_1985; improved finite-sample performance.
* **HC3:** best overall finite-sample performance (@Long_Ervin_2000).
* **HC4:** @Cribari_2004; further improvement under influential observations.

> **R:** `sandwich::vcovHC(lm_obj, type = "HC3")`.

::: {.callout-note}
Besides **Heteroskedasticity Consistent (HC)** estimators, there are also

* ***H*eteroskedasticity and *A*utocorrelation *C*onsistent (HAC)** estimators, as well as estimators that consider
* **clustered error covariances.**

An `R` package that provides H(A)C estimators is `sandwich`.

For clustered covariances, the `clubSandwich` package can be used.
:::

### Robust Inference

#### **Robust Hypothesis Testing: Multiple Parameters**

System of $q$ null hypotheses:
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0: \underset{(q\times K)}{R}\underset{(K\times 1)}{\beta}  = \underset{(q\times 1)}{r^{(0)}}\\
H_1: \underset{(q\times K)}{R}\underset{(K\times 1)}{\beta}  \neq \underset{(q\times 1)}{r^{(0)}}
\end{aligned}
$$

* $R$ ($q\times K$) and $r^{(0)}$ ($q\times 1$) are chosen by the statistician.
* Require $\operatorname{rank}(R)=q$ (no redundant equations).

Unlike the small-sample test (@sec-testmultp), this version is **heteroskedasticity robust**:
$$
\begin{aligned}
W&=n(R\hat\beta_n - r^{(0)})^{\top}[R\,S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\,R^{\top}]^{-1}(R\hat\beta_n-r^{(0)})\\[2ex]
W&\overset{H_0}{\to}_d\chi^2(q), \quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-Ftestasymp}

* Valid only **asymptotically:** use for "largish" $n.$
* In case of homoskedastic errors: substitute 
$$
S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}
$$ 
by 
$$
s_{ub}^2S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
# Finite-sample correction
Instead of $W$ statistic and the $\chi^2(q)$ distribution use the $\frac{W}{q}$ statistic and the $F_{q,n-K}$ distribution for inference.

* Asymptotically ($n\to\infty$): $F_{q,n-K}$ and $\frac{1}{q}\chi^2(q)$ agree.
* For finite $n$: using $\frac{W}{q}$ and $F_{q,n-K}$ gives more conservative test decisions compensating for the estimation error in $S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}$ (or $s_{ub}^2S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}$).
:::

#### **Robust Hypothesis Testing: Single Parameters**

Hypotheses about a single parameter $\beta_k,$ $k=1,\dots,K$:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
H_0: & \beta_k=\beta_k^{(0)}\\
H_1: & \beta_k\ne \beta_k^{(0)}
\end{array}
$$

Select the $k$th diagonal element of @eq-Ftestasymp and take the square root:
$$
T=\frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\beta}_k-\beta_k^{(0)}\right)}{\sqrt{\left[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right]_{(k,k)}}}
\qquad\qquad
T\overset{H_0}{\to}_d\mathcal{N}(0,1),\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$

* $\left[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right]_{(k,k)}$: the $(k,k)$ element of that $K\times K$ matrix.
* This $t$-test statistic allows for **heteroskedastic** error terms.
* Homoskedastic errors: substitute by $s_{ub}^2[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}]_{(k,k)}$.

::: {.callout-tip}
# Finite-sample correction
Use the $t_{(n-K)}$ distribution ($n-K$ degrees of freedom) instead of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

* Asymptotically ($n\to\infty$): $t_{(n-K)}$ and $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ agree.
* For finite $n$: $t_{(n-K)}$ gives larger critical values -- compensates for the estimation error in $[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}]_{(k,k)}$ (or $s_{ub}^2[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}]_{(k,k)}$).
:::

#### **Robust Confidence Intervals**

Following @sec-CIsmallsample, but with robust standard errors, the heteroskedasticity robust $(1-\alpha)\cdot 100\%$ confidence interval is:
$$
\operatorname{CI}^{\text{rob}}_{k,n,1-\alpha}=
\left[\hat\beta_k\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-K}\sqrt{n^{-1}\left[S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\widehat{E}(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})S^{-1}_{X^{\top}X}\right]_{(k,k)}}\right].
$$
The coverage probability is *asymptotic*:
$$
P(\beta_k\in\operatorname{CI}^{\text{rob}}_{k,n,1-\alpha})\to 1-\alpha\quad\text{as}\quad n\to\infty.
$$

## Monte Carlo Simulations {#sec-MCLS}

Data generating process:
$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i &=\beta_1+\beta_2X_{i2}+\beta_3X_{i3}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,n\\
\beta &=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)^{\top}=(2,3,4)^{\top}\\
X_{i2}&\sim U[-4,4]\\
X_{i3}&\sim U[-5,5]\\
\varepsilon_i|X_i&\sim U[-0.5 |X_{i2}|, 0.5 |X_{i2}|],
\end{aligned}
$$
with $(Y_i,X_i)$ i.i.d. across $i=1,\dots,n$, and $X_{i2}$, $X_{i3}$ independent of each other.

Unlike @sec-PSSI, the error term here is **non-Gaussian** and **heteroskedastic**:
$$
Var(\varepsilon_i|X_i)=\frac{1}{12}X_{i2}^2.
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
# Unconditional variance (law of total variance)
$$
\begin{aligned}
Var(\varepsilon_i)
&=E(Var(\varepsilon_i|X_i))+Var(E(\varepsilon_i|X_i))\\
&=E\left(\frac{1}{12}X_{i2}^2\right)+0\\
&=\frac{1}{12}\;Var\left(X_{i2}\right)\quad\text{(since $E(X_{i2})=0$)}\\
&=\frac{1}{12}\left(\frac{1}{12}(4-(-4))^2\right)=\frac{4}{9}.
\end{aligned}
$$
(Using the variance formula for uniform random variables.)
:::

`R`-function to generate data from this DGP:
```{r}
## Function to generate artificial data
myDataGenerator <- function(n, beta){
  ##
  X   <- cbind(rep(1, n),
                 runif(n, -4, 4),
                 runif(n, -5, 5))
  ##
  eps  <- runif(n, min = - 0.5 * abs(X[,2]),
                   max = + 0.5 * abs(X[,2]))
  Y    <- X %*% beta + eps
  ##
  data <- data.frame("Y"   = Y,
                     "X_1" = X[,1],
                     "X_2" = X[,2],
                     "X_3" = X[,3])
  ##
  return(data)
}
```


### Check: Distribution of $\hat\beta_n$

This DGP satisfies our chapter's assumptions. By theory, $\hat\beta_k$ should be approximately normal for large $n$:
$$
\sqrt{n}\left(\hat\beta_{n,k}-\beta_k\right)\to_d\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left[\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\right]_{(k,k)}\right)
$$
$$
\Rightarrow\qquad\hat\beta_{n,k}\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\left(\beta_k, \;n^{-1}\;\left[\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}\right]_{(k,k)}\right).
$$


```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library("fractional")
moment_fun <- function(m=3, a, b){fractional((b^(m+1)-a^(m+1))/((m+1)*(b-a)))}
moment_fun(m=4, a=-4,b=4)
fractional((1/12)*(256/5))
```

For this DGP, all population quantities are known:

* From the distributions of $X_{i2}$, $X_{i3}$:
$$
\Sigma_{X^{\top}X}=E(X_iX_i^{\top})=\left(\begin{matrix}1&0&0\\0&\frac{16}{3}&0\\0&0&\frac{25}{3}\end{matrix}\right).
$$
(Using $E(X^2)=Var(X)$ for mean-zero $X$, and $Var(U[a,b])=\frac{1}{12}(b-a)^2$.)

* And:
$$
E(\varepsilon^2_iX_iX_i^{\top})=E\left(X_iX_i^{\top}\left(\frac{1}{12}X_{i2}^2\right)\right)=\left(\begin{matrix}\frac{4}{9}&0&0\\0&\frac{64}{15}&0\\0&0&\frac{100}{27}\end{matrix}\right).
$$
(Using $E(X^k)=\frac{b^{k+1}-a^{k+1}}{(k+1)(b-a)}$ for $X\sim U[a,b]$; see [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_uniform_distribution).)

For $\hat{\beta}_2$, the theoretical large-sample distribution:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta_{n,2}\overset{a}{\sim}&\mathcal{N}\left(\beta_2, \;\frac{1}{n}\;\left[\left(\begin{matrix}1&0&0\\0&\frac{16}{3}&0\\0&0&\frac{25}{3}\end{matrix}\right)^{-1}\left(\begin{matrix}\frac{4}{9}&0&0\\0&\frac{64}{15}&0\\0&0&\frac{100}{27}\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}1&0&0\\0&\frac{16}{3}&0\\0&0&\frac{25}{3}\end{matrix}\right)^{-1}\right]_{22}\right)\\[2ex]
\hat\beta_{n,2}\overset{a}{\sim}&\mathcal{N}\left(\beta_2, \;\frac{1}{n}\;\left[
  \left(
  \begin{matrix}
  0.444 & 0 &0\\
  0 & 0.15 &0\\
  0&0&0.053
  \end{matrix}\right)\right]_{22}\right)\\[2ex]
\hat\beta_{n,2}\overset{a}{\sim}&\mathcal{N}\left(\beta_2, \;\frac{1}{n}\;0.15\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
**Monte Carlo check:** does the asymptotic distribution of $\hat\beta_2$ already work well at $n=100$?


First, we check the Monte Carlo approximated finite sample $(n=100)$ mean and variance of $\widehat{\beta}_{n,2}$ using 5000 simulated realizations and compare them with the true (usually unknown) large sample population mean and variance 

* $E(\widehat{\beta}_{n,2})=\beta_2=3$
* $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_{n,2}\mid X)=\frac{1}{n}0.15$

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n           <- 100      # a largish sample size
beta_true   <- c(2,3,4) # true data vector

## Mean and variance of the true asymptotic
## normal distribution of beta_hat_2:
# true mean
beta_true_2     <- beta_true[2]
# true variance
var_true_beta_2 <- 0.15 / n

## Let's generate 5000 realizations from beta_hat_2, and check
## whether their distribution is close to the true normal
## distribution.
## (We don't condition on X since the theoretical limit
## distribution is unconditional on X)
rep        <- 5000 # MC replications
beta_hat_2 <- rep(NA, times=rep)
##
for(r in 1:rep){
    MC_data <- myDataGenerator(n    = n,
                               beta = beta_true)
    lm_obj        <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)
    beta_hat_2[r] <- coef(lm_obj)[2]
}

## Compare:
## True beta_2 versus average of beta_hat_2 estimates
c(beta_true_2, round(mean(beta_hat_2), 4))
```
**Good!** The Monte Carlo approximated finite sample mean of $\widehat{\beta}_{n,2}$ effectively equals the theoretical large sample mean $E(\widehat{\beta}_{n,2})=3$.

```{r}
## True variance of beta_hat_2 versus
## empirical variance of beta_hat_2 estimates
c(round(var_true_beta_2, 5), round(var(beta_hat_2), 5))
```
**Great!** The Monte Carlo approximated finite sample variance effectively equals the theoretical large sample variance 
$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_{n,2}\mid X)=0.15/n=0.0015.$

That is, for $n=100,$ the first two moments (mean and variance) of the finite-sample distribution of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ match those of the theoretical asymptotic (large sample) distribution of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}.$

But the first two moments are only two (albeit important) features of a distribution. Next, we check whether the total finite sample $(n=100)$ density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ matches the theoretical asymptotic (large sample) density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}.$


```{r, fig.align="center", echo=TRUE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, out.width = "1\\textwidth"}
## True normal distribution of beta_hat_2 versus
## empirical density of beta_hat_2 estimates
library("scales")
curve(expr = dnorm(x,
                   mean = beta_true_2,
                   sd   = sqrt(var_true_beta_2)),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col  = gray(.2), lwd=3, lty=1,
      xlim = range(beta_hat_2),
      ylim = c(0,14.1),main=paste0("n=",n))

lines(density(beta_hat_2,
              bw = bw.SJ(beta_hat_2)),
      col = alpha("blue",.5), lwd = 3)

legend("topleft", lty=c(1,1), lwd = c(3,3),
     col=c(gray(.2), alpha("blue",.5)), bty="n",
     legend=
     c(expression(
       "Theoretical (Asymptotic) Gaussian Density of"~hat(beta)[2]),
      expression(
       "Empirical Density Estimation based on MC realizations from"~hat(beta)[2])))
```
**Great!** For $n=100,$ the Monte Carlo approximated finite sample density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ matches the theoretical asymptotic normal density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ really very well. 

**Does this also work for small $n$, e.g. $n=5$?**
```{r}
set.seed(123)
n           <- 5       # a small sample size
beta_true   <- c(2,3,4) # true data vector

## Mean and variance of the true asymptotic
## normal distribution of beta_hat_2:
# true mean
beta_true_2     <- beta_true[2]
# true variance
var_true_beta_2 <- 0.15 / n

## Let's generate 5000 realizations from beta_hat_2, and check
## whether their distribution is close to the true normal
## distribution.
## (We don't condition on X since the theoretical limit
## distribution is unconditional on X)
rep        <- 5000 # MC replications
beta_hat_2 <- rep(NA, times=rep)
##
for(r in 1:rep){
    MC_data <- myDataGenerator(n    = n,
                               beta = beta_true)
    lm_obj        <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)
    beta_hat_2[r] <- coef(lm_obj)[2]
}

## Compare:
## True beta_2 versus average of beta_hat_2 estimates
c(beta_true_2, round(mean(beta_hat_2), 4))
```
**OK:** The Monte Carlo approximated finite-sample $(n=5)$ mean sill effectively equals the theoretical large-sample mean of $\widehat{\beta}_{n,2}.$

```{r}
## True variance of beta_hat_2 versus
## empirical variance of beta_hat_2 estimates
c(round(var_true_beta_2, 4), round(var(beta_hat_2), 4))
```
**Ouch!** The Monte Carlo approximated finite-sample $(n=5)$ variance is about 50% smaller than the theoretical large-sample variance of $\widehat{\beta}_{n,2}.$

$\Rightarrow$ **Large-sample results don't simply carry over to small samples.**

* Reason: the LLN hasn't kicked in yet; the variability in $S_{X^{\top}X}^{-1}$ is not negligible.

This issue, is also visible when comparing the Monte Carlo approximated finite-sample $(n=5)$ density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ against the theoretical large-sample density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}.$

```{r, fig.align="center", echo=TRUE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, out.width = "1\\textwidth"}
## True normal distribution of beta_hat_2 versus
## empirical density of beta_hat_2 estimates
library("scales")
curve(expr = dnorm(x,
                   mean = beta_true_2,
                   sd   = sqrt(var_true_beta_2)),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col  = gray(.2), lwd = 3, lty = 1,
      xlim = c(2,4),
      ylim = c(0,3), main=paste0("n=",n))

lines(density(beta_hat_2,
              bw = bw.SJ(beta_hat_2)),
      col = alpha("blue",.5), lwd = 3)

## Legend
legend("topleft", lty=c(1,1), lwd=c(3,3),
       col=c(gray(.2), alpha("blue",.5)), bty="n",
       legend=
c(expression(
  "Theoretical (Asymptotic) Gaussian Density of"~hat(beta)[2]),
  expression(
  "Empirical Density Estimation based on MC realizations from"~
  hat(beta)[2])))
```
**Not good:** For $n=5,$ the Monte Carlo approximated finite-sample density of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}$ has substantially fatter tails than the theoretical large sample distribution of $\widehat\beta_{n,2}.$ 

$\Rightarrow$ using the quantiles of the large sample distribution would lead to **over-rejections**; i.e. 
$$
\text{Type I error rate} >\alpha
$$ 
leading to invalid statistical inference. 

**Fortunately:** asymptotics kick in fast here. When you play with the code, you'll see that the large sample distribution effectively matches the actual finite-sample distribution for sample sizes $n\geq 15.$




### Check: Testing Multiple Parameters

Test the (here correct) null hypothesis:
\begin{align*}
H_0:\;&\beta_2=3\quad\text{and}\quad\beta_3=4\\
\text{versus}\quad H_1:\;&\beta_2\neq 3\quad\text{and/or}\quad\beta_3\neq 4.
\end{align*}
Equivalently:
\begin{align*}
H_0:\;&R\beta -r^{(0)} = 0 \\
H_1:\;&R\beta -r^{(0)} \neq 0,
\end{align*}
with
$$
R=\left(
\begin{matrix}
0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
\end{matrix}\right)\quad\text{ and }\quad
r^{(0)}=\left(\begin{matrix}3\\4\\\end{matrix}\right).
$$
`R` code for this test, using HC3 robust variance `sandwich::vcovHC(lm_obj, type="HC3")`:
```{r}
suppressMessages(library("car")) # for linearHypothesis()
# ?linearHypothesis
library("sandwich") # for vcovHC(), robust variance estimations

set.seed(1009)

## Generate data
MC_data <- myDataGenerator(n    = 100,
                           beta = beta_true)

## Estimate the linear regression model parameters
lm_obj <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)

vcovHC3_mat <- sandwich::vcovHC(lm_obj, type="HC3")

## Option 1:
# car::linearHypothesis(model = lm_obj,
#                       hypothesis.matrix = c("X_2=3", "X_3=4"),
#                       vcov = vcovHC3_mat)

## Option 2:
R <- rbind(c(0,1,0),
           c(0,0,1))
car::linearHypothesis(model = lm_obj,
                      hypothesis.matrix = R,
                      rhs  = c(3,4),
                      vcov = vcovHC3_mat)
```
The $p$-value is larger than any typical significance level $\alpha.$ So, we cannot reject $H_0.$  That's good news, since $H_0$ is correct here (rejecting it would be a type I error).

On average, over many resamplings, some false rejections will occur, but the rate of those Type I errors must stay $\leq\alpha.$ The following code chunck checks whether the Monte Carlo approximated finite sample $(n=100)$ probability of a Type I error remains bounded from above by the chosen nominal $\alpha=0.05$ level. 

```{r}
set.seed(1110)

B        <- 10000
p_values <- numeric(B)

for(r in 1:B){
  MC_data     <- myDataGenerator(n    = 100, beta = beta_true)
  lm_obj      <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)
  vcovHC3_mat <- sandwich::vcovHC(lm_obj, type="HC3")
  Ftest       <- car::linearHypothesis(model = lm_obj,
                        hypothesis.matrix = c("X_2=3", "X_3=4"),
                        vcov = vcovHC3_mat)
  p_values[r] <- Ftest$'Pr(>F)'[2]
}
## Nominal type I error rate
alpha <- 0.05
## Empirical type I error rate
length(p_values[p_values < alpha])/B
```

**Good!** The Monte Carlo approximated finite sample $(n=100)$ probability of a Type I error effectively equals the chosen nominal $\alpha=0.05$ level. 

### Check: Testing Single Parameters

Test a single parameter:
\begin{align*}
H_0:&\beta_3=4\\
\text{versus}\quad H_1:&\beta_3\neq 4.
\end{align*}
```{r}
# Load libraries
suppressMessages(library("lmtest"))  # for coeftest()

## Generate data
n <- 100
MC_data <- myDataGenerator(n    = n,
                           beta = beta_true)

## Estimate the linear regression model parameters
lm_obj <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)

## Robust t test

## Robust standard error for \hat{\beta}_3:
SE_rob <- sqrt(vcovHC(lm_obj, type = "HC3")[3,3])
## hypothetical (H0) value of \beta_3:
beta_3_H0 <- 4
## estimate for beta_3:
beta_3_hat <- coef(lm_obj)[3]
## robust t-test statistic
t_test_stat <- (beta_3_hat - beta_3_H0)/SE_rob
## p-value
K <- length(coef(lm_obj))
##
p_value <- 2 * min(   pt(q = t_test_stat, df = n - K),
                   1- pt(q = t_test_stat, df = n - K))
p_value
```
**Again:** The $p$-value is larger than any typical significance level $\alpha.$ So, we cannot reject $H_0.$  That's good news, since $H_0$ is correct here (rejecting it would be a type I error).


Let's check the Monte Carlo approximated finite sample probability of a type I error:


```{r}
set.seed(1009)
n        <- 100
B        <- 10000
p_values <- numeric(B)

for(r in 1:B){
  MC_data     <- myDataGenerator(n = n, beta = beta_true)
  lm_obj      <- lm(Y ~ X_2 + X_3, data = MC_data)
  SE_rob      <- sqrt(vcovHC(lm_obj, type = "HC3")[3,3])
  beta_3_hat  <- coef(lm_obj)[3]
  ## robust t-test statistic
  t_test_stat <- (beta_3_hat - beta_3_H0)/SE_rob
  p_values[r] <- 2 * min(   pt(q = t_test_stat, df = n - length(beta_true)),
                         1- pt(q = t_test_stat, df = n - length(beta_true)))
}
## Nominal type I error rate
alpha <- 0.05
## Empirical type I error rate
length(p_values[p_values < alpha])/B
```

**Good!** The empirical type I error rate effectively equals the nominal $\alpha=0.05$ level. 

## Real Data Example {#sec-RDLSInf}

We revisit the data example from @sec-RDSSInf, but now allow for heteroskedastic, non-Gaussian errors.

```{r}
## The AER package contains a lot of datasets
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(AER))

## Attach the DoctorVisits data to make it usable
data("DoctorVisits")

lm_obj <- lm(visits ~ gender + age + income, data = DoctorVisits)
```

Regression model:
$$
Y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_{gender} X_{gender,i}
              + \beta_{age} X_{age,i}
              + \beta_{income} X_{income,i} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i=1,\dots,n
$$

* $X_{gender,i}=1$ if subject $i$ is a woman, $0$ if a man
* $X_{age,i}$: age of subject $i$, in years $/100$
* $X_{income,i}$: annual income of subject $i$, in tens of thousands of dollars

Heteroskedasticity-robust inference: 

* `sandwich::vcovHC()` HC3 robust variance estimation
* `lmtest::coeftest()` Coefficient/inference table

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
## No robust standard errors:
coeftest(lm_obj)
## HC3 robust standard errors:
coeftest(lm_obj, vcov = vcovHC(lm_obj, type = "HC3"))
```

Alternative: `stargazer`, for (almost) publication-ready tables, with and without robust SEs:
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, results='asis'}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("stargazer"))

# Adjust standard errors
cov_beta_HC3   <- vcovHC(lm_obj, type = "HC3")
robust_HC3_se  <- sqrt(diag(cov_beta_HC3))

# Stargazer output (with and without RSE)
stargazer(lm_obj, lm_obj,
          se   = list(NULL, robust_HC3_se),
          column.labels = c("", "Robust SE"),
          type = "html") # alternatively: type = "text" or type = "latex"
```

* `DoctorVisits` is a single cross-section $\Rightarrow$ HC-type SEs are appropriate.
* For time series or panel data: swap in `vcovHAC()` or `vcovCL()` -- same `coeftest(lm_obj, vcov = ...)` pattern.
